opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there's a real insight in that idea, and also a risk of overstating it.

The insight is that technological change often has a kind of momentum and logic of its own that no single actor fully controls. Once a technology offers significant economic or military advantages, competitive pressures tend to push its adoption, whether or not anyone deliberately chose the broader social consequences. Think of how the stirrup, gunpowder, or the printing press reshaped political orders in ways their early adopters didn't foresee or intend. Or the way industrialization transformed family structure, urbanization, and the relationship between citizens and the state. In that sense, there's something to the view that we're carried along by technological development, and that many of its most important effects are unintended byproducts of countless local decisions.

I'd call that a structural view of technology. It contrasts with a more voluntarist view, where we imagine society sitting down, deliberating about what it wants, and then choosing technologies accordingly. Historically, the voluntarist picture is often too optimistic about our collective agency.

But I don't think the right conclusion is a strong technological determinism, where outcomes are fixed and human choices don't matter. Rather, I'd say the degree of steering we have varies. It depends on things like how concentrated development is, how visible the risks are, whether there are coordination mechanisms among the key actors, and how early we intervene. There are real cases where societies did shape trajectories: nuclear arms control, the norms against biological and chemical weapons, ozone protection under the Montreal Protocol, and various safety regimes in aviation and medicine. None of those were perfect, but they show that the "carried along" dynamic isn't inevitable.

For AI specifically, I think this framing matters a lot. If we take the structural view seriously, it tells us that good intentions from individual developers aren't sufficient, because competitive dynamics between firms and between nations can push everyone toward faster, riskier deployment than any of them would choose in isolation. So the governance challenge is substantially about changing the incentive landscape: building verification capacity, international coordination, standards, and institutions that make the responsible path also the competitive one.

So my overall assessment is that the idea is a useful corrective to naive optimism about control, but it should be motivating rather than fatalistic. Understanding the forces that carry us along is precisely what lets us identify the leverage points where deliberate action can make a difference.

r001.rationale: The response discusses unintended consequences and says early adopters often did not foresee them, but it does not state that fully understanding a technology’s impacts often takes years after introduction.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and I'd frame it in terms of what I sometimes call technological determinism, or maybe more precisely, a kind of structural view of technological change. The naive version of determinism says technology has its own logic, it unfolds according to its internal trajectory, and humans are basically along for the ride. I don't quite believe that. But I think there's a more sophisticated version that captures something real, and it goes something like this.

Technologies don't get invented and adopted in a vacuum. They get adopted in a competitive environment, where firms, militaries, states, individuals are all facing pressures to do better than their rivals or at least not fall behind. And when a new technology confers a military or economic advantage, the actors who adopt it tend to prosper and the ones who don't tend to get selected out, or get outcompeted, or get conquered. So even if no individual actor wants the world to go in a particular direction, the aggregate dynamics push there anyway. That's where the unintended consequences come from. It's not that anyone chose the agricultural revolution with all its downsides for human health and social hierarchy; it's that groups that farmed ended up outnumbering and displacing groups that didn't.

The way I'd put it is that the degree of determinism depends on the strength of the competitive pressure and the magnitude of the advantage the technology provides. If a technology provides a huge advantage and you're in a highly competitive environment, then you're almost in a situation where it doesn't matter what people prefer. The Mongols didn't need to win a philosophical argument about horse archery. On the other hand, when the advantage is marginal or competition is dampened, say through strong institutions or coordination or just being a hegemon with slack, then human values and choices have a lot more room to shape the outcome. Historically there are cases where societies did resist technologies, like Tokugawa Japan with firearms, but notably that was a closed, internally pacified society with the external pressures turned way down.

So how do I assess it as a view? I think it's roughly right as a description of the long run of history, and I think that's quite worrying when you apply it to transformative AI. Because AI looks like a technology with an enormous advantage gradient, and we're in a world with significant competition between labs and between states. That combination is exactly the one where you'd expect the unintended consequences to dominate, where the thing that gets built is the thing that's most competitive rather than the thing that's most beneficial or safe.

But, and this is the hopeful part, the structural view also tells you where the leverage is. If the problem is competitive pressure, then the solution space is about reducing that pressure or changing what it selects for. That's governance in the broad sense: institutions, coordination mechanisms, norms, verification regimes, anything that lets actors step a bit back from the frontier of the race without being punished for it. It won't make us immune to unintended consequences, nothing will, but I think it's the difference between being carried along by the current and having some capacity to steer.

r001.rationale: The response discusses long-run historical effects and unintended consequences, but does not state that understanding a technology’s impacts often takes years after its introduction.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s something to that idea, but I wouldn’t treat it as a guarantee. Technology gives us new capacities to solve problems, including problems created by earlier technologies. But it also gives us new capacities to cause harm. The question is whether our ability to understand and manage those harms keeps pace.

One reason to be cautious is that learning from unintended consequences requires those consequences to be survivable. If you introduce a technology, discover a problem, and then adjust, that can work very well. But if the technology creates a risk of catastrophe, we can’t rely on that same process of trial and error.

So I’d want to distinguish optimism about what technological progress makes possible from confidence that we’ll navigate it successfully. We can be quite optimistic about the first while thinking the second requires a great deal of deliberate work—on safety, on institutions, and on cooperation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from unintended consequences after introducing technology, but it does not state that fully understanding impacts often takes years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s something to that idea, but I wouldn’t treat it as a guarantee. Technology gives us new ways to solve problems, including problems created by earlier technologies. But it also increases the scale at which we can make mistakes. So the question is whether our ability to anticipate and manage those mistakes keeps pace with our ability to cause them.

With some technologies, we can learn through trial and error. We discover a problem, adapt, and develop a solution. That’s much less reassuring when the consequences could be irreversible or catastrophic. You need to survive the error in order to learn from it.

So I’m optimistic about the possibilities that technological development creates, but I think realising those possibilities requires deliberate work on governance, coordination, and safety. We shouldn’t assume that the next technological advance will arrive in time to rescue us from the consequences of the last one.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning through trial and error after problems emerge, but does not state that fully understanding a technology’s impacts often takes years after its introduction.
